The Constitution of the German Reich ( German : Die Verfassung des Deutschen Reichs ), usually known as the Weimar Constitution ( Weimarer Verfassung ), was the constitution that governed Germany during the Weimar Republic era. The constitution created a federal semi-presidential republic [ 1 ] with a parliament whose lower house, the Reichstag , was elected by universal suffrage using proportional representation . The appointed upper house, the Reichsrat , represented the interests of the federal states. The president of Germany had supreme command over the military, extensive emergency powers, and appointed and removed the chancellor, who was responsible to the Reichstag. The constitution included a significant number of civic rights such as freedom of speech and habeas corpus . It guaranteed freedom of religion and did not permit the establishment of a state church.
